issues.legal_issue: The amendment defining village common land encompasses land reserved for common purposes during consolidation from proprietors’ holdings outside their permissible ceiling limits, and is constitutionally valid as a declaratory measure of agrarian reform.
material_facts: During consolidation, land was reserved for common purposes by applying a pro-rata cut to proprietors’ holdings; the land at issue was outside the proprietors’ permissible ceiling limits.
The Supreme Court had previously held that land reserved in this manner vested in the Panchayat as part of agrarian reform and that compensation was not payable.
The challenged amendment was enacted after receiving the President’s assent.
issues.conclusion: The amendment is valid and clarifies the existing legal position: land reserved for common purposes from holdings outside the permissible ceiling limits had already vested in the Panchayat and was not newly acquired by the amendment.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A protects laws forming part of agrarian reform, including an amendment that extends or clarifies the operation of an existing agrarian-reform law when it receives presidential assent. Article 300A does not require compensation where the land had already vested in the Panchayat. The Court relied on Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, which treated land reserved by pro-rata cut outside the applicable ceiling limits as acquired for agrarian reform without compensation, and Mahant Sankarshan Ramanuja Das Goswami v. State of Orissa, on Article 31A’s protection for an assented amending Act.

rule.if: challenge_to_common_land_amendment and land_reserved_by_pro_rata_cut and land_outside_permissible_ceiling and amendment_received_presidential_assent

predicates.challenge_to_common_land_amendment: A proceeding challenges a law that defines or regulates village common land.
predicates.land_reserved_by_pro_rata_cut: During consolidation, land was set aside for village common purposes by taking a proportionate share from proprietors’ holdings.
predicates.land_outside_permissible_ceiling: The land taken for common purposes was outside the permissible ceiling limits applicable to the proprietors.
predicates.amendment_received_presidential_assent: The amending law received the required assent before it took effect.

issues.definition: When a challenged common-land amendment with presidential assent concerns pro-rata land reserved outside the permissible ceiling limits, the amendment is valid and the land is treated as already vested in the Panchayat.

issues.legal_issue: For land reserved for common purposes from proprietors’ holdings within their permissible ceiling limits, vesting in the Panchayat transfers management and control, not title, and the land remains dedicated to village common purposes.
material_facts: Some land reserved during consolidation by pro-rata cut fell within the permissible ceiling limits applicable to the proprietors.
The land was set aside for common purposes benefiting the village community, including the proprietors.
The consolidation scheme did not transfer ownership of this category of land to the Panchayat.
issues.conclusion: Only management and control of this land vest in the Panchayat; the proprietors’ title is not transferred, but the land cannot be reclaimed or sold as if it were available for private redistribution.
issues.legal_principle: Under the second proviso to Article 31A(1), acquisition of personally cultivated land within the applicable ceiling limits requires compensation at not less than market value. Applying Ajit Singh v. State of Punjab, the Court held that where title remains with the proprietary body and the Panchayat manages the land for common needs and benefits, only management and control vest in the Panchayat. Common purposes may include present and future village needs, and the management and control are not a basis for reversion or sale of the land.

rule.if: challenge_to_common_land_vesting and land_reserved_by_pro_rata_cut and land_within_permissible_ceiling and land_set_aside_for_village_common_purposes

predicates.challenge_to_common_land_vesting: A proceeding challenges the effect of setting aside land for village common purposes.
predicates.land_reserved_by_pro_rata_cut: During consolidation, land was set aside for village common purposes by taking a proportionate share from proprietors’ holdings.
predicates.land_within_permissible_ceiling: The land taken for common purposes fell within the permissible ceiling limits applicable to the proprietors.
predicates.land_set_aside_for_village_common_purpos: The land was reserved to serve common needs or benefits of the village community.

issues.definition: When land within proprietors’ permissible ceiling limits is taken by pro-rata cut for village common purposes, the Panchayat manages and controls it while title remains with the proprietors and the land stays dedicated to those purposes.

issues.legal_issue: Land reserved for common purposes does not become distributable among proprietors merely because it is unused at a particular time or has not yet been put to its reserved use.
material_facts: The land had been reserved for common purposes in a consolidation scheme.
Some of that land had not been put to a common use when the proprietors sought its redistribution.
The scheme did not impose a deadline for using reserved land, and village requirements could change over time.
issues.conclusion: Unused land reserved for common purposes cannot be treated as surplus land available for redistribution among proprietors.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated common purposes as dynamic and encompassing both present and future requirements of the village community. Land reserved for common purposes remains so reserved whether or not it has yet been used, and it cannot be redistributed merely because it is presently unused. The Court rejected the contrary approach in the cited High Court decisions, including the conclusion on Bachat land in Jai Singh II.

predicates.dispute_over_redistribution_of_reserved_: A proceeding concerns a claim to redistribute land that was set aside during consolidation.
predicates.land_reserved_for_common_purposes: The land was set aside in a consolidation scheme for common needs or benefits of the village community.
predicates.land_not_currently_used_for_common_purpo: The land is not presently being put to a common use.

issues.definition: If reserved village common land is not currently being used, it nevertheless cannot be redistributed to proprietors solely on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A dispute over whether land recorded under joint proprietary descriptions was reserved for common purposes is for determination by the authority under the village common lands law, rather than by a civil court.
material_facts: The dispute concerned land recorded using descriptions of joint proprietary ownership.
The parties disputed whether the land had actually been reserved for common purposes during consolidation.
The Court held that revenue-record descriptions alone did not resolve whether the land was reserved for common purposes.
issues.conclusion: The authority and procedures under the village common lands law determine whether such land was reserved for common purposes and the related dispute over rights, title, or interest; the contrary view that a civil court is the available forum was not accepted.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Sections 2(g) and 13A of the 1961 Act and the machinery provided under that Act to determine disputes concerning land vested or deemed vested in a Panchayat, including whether land recorded as Jumla Mushtarka Malkan or similar descriptions was reserved for common purposes. It rejected the contrary forum conclusion in Parkash Singh v. Joint Development Commissioner, Punjab, and applied the statutory scheme rather than treating the revenue entry as determinative.

predicates.dispute_over_common_land_title_or_status: A proceeding disputes rights, title, interest, or the legal status of land claimed to be village common land.
predicates.land_has_joint_proprietary_revenue_entry: The revenue record describes the land using a joint proprietary ownership entry.
predicates.parties_dispute_common_purpose_reservati: The parties disagree about whether the land was reserved for common purposes during consolidation.

issues.definition: When jointly recorded land is disputed as to whether it was reserved for common purposes, the common-land authority determines that status.

issues.legal_issue: A superior court’s limited alteration of an appealed order does not make the lower court’s unadopted reasoning a declaration of law by the superior court.
material_facts: An appeal concerned a High Court judgment about redistribution of unused land.
The Supreme Court removed only the High Court’s direction imposing a time limit for redistribution proceedings.
The Supreme Court did not consider or approve the High Court’s reasoning on whether unused land could be redistributed.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s reasoning was not affirmed as a Supreme Court precedent; only the operative order resulting from the Supreme Court’s limited alteration governed.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of merger concerns the operative part of the order, and the reasoning of the lower court does not become the reasoning of the superior court unless the superior court adopts, reiterates, or expressly approves it. A declaration of law under Article 141 requires a decision that expressly or necessarily considers the point. The Court relied on Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala, S. Shanmugavel Nadar v. State of Tamil Nadu, V.M. Salgaocar & Bros. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and Kaikhosrou (Chick) Kavasji Framji v. Union of India.

predicates.appeal_against_lower_court_order: A party appeals a lower court’s order to a superior court.
predicates.higher_court_alters_only_a_limited_part: The superior court changes only a limited operative direction in the order.
predicates.higher_court_does_not_consider_or_adopt_: The superior court neither considers the relevant reasoning on its merits nor adopts or expressly approves it.

issues.definition: If a superior court changes only a limited part of an order without considering or adopting the lower court’s reasoning, that reasoning does not become a binding declaration of law by the superior court.

issues.legal_issue: Legislation transferring village common land to a municipality is not protected as agrarian reform when the transfer is not directed toward agrarian reform.
material_facts: Amendments to municipal laws provided for village common land to vest in municipalities.
The challenged transfer was not directed toward agrarian reform.
The High Court had held the relevant municipal common-land legislation unconstitutional for lack of the character of agrarian reform.
issues.conclusion: The Court affirmed that the challenged municipal amendments were unconstitutional because they were not part of agrarian reform.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects laws providing for agrarian reform, not a municipal transfer of village common land that is not directed toward agrarian reform. The Court applied the reasoning of the Full Bench decision in Rajender Parshad v. State of Haryana, which had struck down the municipal common-land legislation on that basis.

predicates.challenge_to_municipal_common_land_law: A proceeding challenges a law governing the transfer of village common land to a municipality.
predicates.law_transfers_village_common_land_to_mun: The challenged law provides for village common land to vest in a municipality.
predicates.transfer_is_not_agrarian_reform: The transfer is not directed toward agrarian reform.

issues.definition: When a challenged law transfers village common land to a municipality without being directed toward agrarian reform, the law is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: When village land enters municipal limits, the land reserved for common purposes transfers to municipal control rather than reverting to proprietors, and inclusion of part of a village area is sufficient.
material_facts: Land reserved for common purposes was managed or controlled by a Gram Panchayat before the relevant area entered municipal limits.
The municipal boundary could include all or part of a Gram Panchayat area.
The Panchayat and municipal legislation provided for the transfer of the Panchayat’s assets and liabilities when its area became part of a municipality.
The proprietors argued that land would transfer only if the entire village area entered municipal limits and that otherwise it should revert to them.
issues.conclusion: Land reserved for common purposes does not revert to proprietors when a village area enters municipal limits; inclusion of part of the area is sufficient for the land to vest in the municipality.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read Section 7(4) of the Haryana Panchayati Raj Act, 1994 together with the municipal boundary provisions and applied the principle that the greater includes the less. It relied on Notified Area Committee v. Des Raj and Municipal Committee, Sirhind v. Parshotam Dass, which rejected reversion to former proprietors when village land became part of an urban local body, including where only part of the village area was included.

predicates.village_common_land_transition_to_munici: A village area containing land managed or controlled by a Panchayat becomes part of a municipal area.
predicates.land_reserved_for_common_purposes: The land was set aside for common needs or benefits of the village community.
predicates.municipal_boundary_includes_all_or_part_: The municipal boundary includes all or part of the area formerly administered by the Panchayat.

issues.definition: When reserved village common land is within an area brought into municipal limits, whether in whole or in part, it transfers to municipal control and does not revert to proprietors.

issues.legal_issue: The procedure for removing an unauthorized occupant from common-purpose land differs from the procedure for deciding a genuine dispute over rights, title, or interest in that land.
material_facts: The judgment considered a summary eviction law applicable to unauthorized occupation of land reserved for common purposes and the more comprehensive village common lands law.
The latter law empowers the Collector to decide questions of right, title, or interest in land vested or deemed vested in a Panchayat.
The Court distinguished an undisputed unauthorized occupation from a dispute about the nature of the occupation or the parties’ rights in the land.
issues.conclusion: Summary eviction proceedings may be used where occupation is unauthorized and undisputed; where the nature of occupation or rights, title, or interest is disputed, the procedure under the village common lands law must be used.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the summary eviction mechanism under the Haryana Common Purposes Land Eviction and Rent Recovery Act, 1985 from the dispute-resolution jurisdiction under Section 13A of the 1961 Act. The latter provides for determination of disputes over right, title, or interest in land vested or deemed vested in a Panchayat; the summary procedure addresses unauthorized occupation where that issue is not genuinely disputed.

predicates.proceeding_concerns_occupation_of_reserv: A proceeding concerns a person’s occupation of land reserved for village common purposes.
predicates.unauthorized_occupation_is_undisputed: The parties do not genuinely dispute that the occupation is unauthorized.
predicates.nature_of_occupation_or_land_rights_is_d: The parties genuinely dispute the nature of the occupation or their rights, title, or interest in the land.

issues.definition: For occupation of reserved common land, undisputed unauthorized occupation follows the summary eviction route, while a genuine dispute over occupation or land rights follows the common-land dispute procedure.
